2276.subject: Zoology
2276.text:
Assertion : Pharyngeal nephridia play a role in the conservation of water in the earthworm.
Reason : They help the earthworm in keeping the skin moist for cutaneous respiration.
options: If both assertion and reason are true and reason is the correct explanation of assertion
If both assertion and reason are true but reason is not the correct explanation of assertion
If assertion is true but reason is false
If both assertion and reason are false.
2276.sol:
Pharyngeal nephridia occur in three pairs of bunches in the 4 th, 5 th and 6 th segments lying on each side of the alimentary canal. The ducts of the nephridia of the sixth segment open into the buccal cavity while the ducts from the nephridia bunches of the fourth and fifth segments open into the pharynx. These ducts carry excretory products from the pharyngeal nephridia into the gut. Enteronephric condition is an adaptation for the conservation of water which is absorbed by the inner lining of the alimentary canal.
Ectonephric nephridia discharge their contents directly to the outside which help the earthworm in keeping the skin moist for cutaneous respiration only. Integumentary nephridia are ectonephric nephridia while, pharyngeal and septal nephridia are enteronephric.

3436.text:
Which of the following outer octahedral complexes have same number of unpaired electrons?
1. \($\left[\mathrm{MnCl}_{6}\right]^{3-}\)
2. \(\left[\mathrm{FeF}_{6}$\right]^{3-}\)
3. \($\left[\mathrm{CoF}_{6}\right]^{3-}\)
4. \(\left[\mathrm{Ni}\left(\mathrm{NH}_{3}$\right)_6\right]^{2+}\)
3436.sol:
All four complexes given are outer orbital or high spin octahedral complexes. So, \(d\)-orbital electrons of central metal ions of the complexes remain unaffected by weak field ligands.
So, \(d\)-configuration of free \(M^{n+}\) and coordinated \(M^{n+}\) will remain same.
1.
1. \($\left[\mathrm{Mn} \mathrm{Cl}_{6}\right]^{3-} \longrightarrow  \mathrm{Mn}^{3+} \Rightarrowd^4, n=4\)
[ \(\because n=\) Number$ of $unpaired electrons]
2. \(\left[\mathrm{FeF}_{6}$\right]^{3-} \longrightarrow $\mathrm{Fe}^{3+} \Rightarrow$d^5, n=5\)
3. \($\left[\mathrm{CoF}_{6}\right]^{3-} \longrightarrow  \mathrm{Co}^{3+} \Rightarrowd^6, n=4\)
4. \(\left[\mathrm{Ni}\left(\mathrm{NH}_{3}$\right)_6\right]^{2+} \longrightarrow $\mathrm{Ni}^{2+} \Rightarrow$d^3, n=2\)
So, complexes 1 and 3 have same number of unpaired electrons \((n=4)\).

6216.subject: Mathematics
6216.text: Find the equation of a line passing through the point $(4,3)$, which cuts a triangle of minimum area from the first quadrant.
6216.sol:
The equation& of the straight line passing through the point& $\left(4, 3\right)$, whose~slope& $m$~(assume).

$y - 3 = m\left(x - 4\right) ⇒ y = mx - 4m + 3$

So,~$x -$intercept~of the line is& $4 - \dfrac{3}{m}$

and~$y -$intercept is~$3 - 4m$,

So, area of the given triangle is~$A = \dfrac{1}{2} \times \left(4 - \dfrac{3}{m}\right)\left(3 - 4m\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(24 - 16m - \dfrac{9}{m}\right) = 12 - 8m - \dfrac{9}{2m}$

To find the min/max,

$\dfrac{dA}{dm} = 0 ⇒ - 8 + \dfrac{9}{2m^{2}} = 0 ⇒ m = \pm \dfrac{3}{4}$

Second derivative test :

${\dfrac{d^{2}A}{dm^{2}}}_{m} = - \dfrac{9}{m3} ⇒ {\dfrac{d^{2}A}{dm^{2}}}_{m = \dfrac{3}{4}} 0$

Also, the straight line makes triangle in the first quadrant,~so& $m = - \dfrac{3}{4}$

So, the equation of the line~which passes though the given point is

$y - 3 = - \dfrac{3}{4}\left(x - 4\right) ⇒ 4y - 12 = - 3x + 12 ⇒ 3x + 4y = 24$

6273.text: If $f(x)=(2 k+1) x-3-k e^{-x}+2 e^x$ is monotonically increasing for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$, then the least value of $k$ is
6273.sol:
Given,

f(x)=(2 k+1) x-3-k e^{-x}+2 e^x

Since, $f(x)$ is monotonically increasing for all $x \in R$.

So,

$\begin{array}{rlrl}$& & (2 k+1)+k e^{-x}+2 e^x & \geq 0 \\
\Rightarrow & e^{-x}$\left(($2 k+1) e^x+k+2 e^{2 x}\right) & \geq 0 \\
$\text{ or }$& (2 k+1) e^x+k+2 e^{2 x} & \geq 0 \\
\Rightarrow & 2 e^x$\left($e^x+k\right)+1$\left($e^x+k\right) & \geq 0 \\
\Rightarrow & & $\left($2 e^x+1\right)$\left($e^x+k\right) & \geq 0 \\
\Rightarrow & & e^x+k \geq 0 $\text{ or }$k & \geq 0
\end{array}

Hence, least value of $k$ is zero.

$= 2t^{2}e^{t} - 2\left[te^{t} - ∫ e^{t}dt\right] = 2t^{2}e^{t} - 2te^{t} + 2e^{t} + C^{'}$

$= e^{x}\left(2x - 2\sqrt{x} + 2\right) + C^{'}$

Hence, $A + B + C = 2$

Since, angle between $y=m x+c$ and

$y=-3 x+c$
Since, it passes through $(1,2)$.
 $\begin{aligned} & \therefore \quad 2=-3+c \\ & \Rightarrow \quad c=5 \\ & \therefore \quad y=-3 x+5 \\ & \Rightarrow \quad 3 x+y=5 \\ & \end{aligned}$ 
Again, putting $m=\frac{1}{3}  in Eq. (i), we get
$y=-$\frac{x}{3}+$ c$

$\begin{aligned}

& =\mathrm{MB}\left(\cos \theta_1-\cos \theta_2\right) \\
& \therefore \mathrm{KE}=\mathrm{MB} \cos 0^{{}^{\circ}} \\
& =2.5 \times 3 \times 10^{-5} \\
& =7.5 \times 10^{-5} \mathrm{ J}=75 \times 10^{-6} \mu \mathrm{J}
\end{aligned}$

17973.subject: Mathematics
17973.text: An inverted conical flask is being filled with water at the rate of $3{cm}^{3}\sec^{-1}$. The height of the flask is $10$ cm and the radius of the base is $5$ cm. How fast is the water level rising when the level is $4cm ?$
17973.sol:
Let depth of water at time $t$ be $h$ and the radius of the base of water level be $r$.

From similar $∆ OMP$ and $∆ ONQ$, we have

$\dfrac{OM}{ON} = \dfrac{PM}{QN}$

$⇒ \dfrac{h}{10} = \dfrac{r}{5}$

$⇒ r = \dfrac{5h}{10}$

$⇒ r = \dfrac{h}{2}$

We have, $V = \dfrac{1}{3}\pir^{2}h = \dfrac{1}{3}\pi\left(\dfrac{h}{2}\right)2h$

$⇒ V = \dfrac{\pih^{3}}{12}$

On differentiating both sides, we get

$\dfrac{dV}{dt} = \dfrac{\pi}{12} \cdot 3h^{2}\dfrac{dh}{dt} = \dfrac{\pih^{2}}{4}\dfrac{dh}{dt}$

Given, $\dfrac{dV}{dt} = 3{cm}^{3}\sec^{-1}$ when $h = 4cm,$ so we get

$3 = \dfrac{\pi \times {4}^{2}}{4}\dfrac{dh}{dt}$

$⇒ \dfrac{dh}{dt} = \dfrac{3}{4\pi}cm\sec^{-1}$

Hence, the water level is rising at $\dfrac{3}{4\pi}cm\sec^{-1}$

$∴$ Option (b) is correct.

19629.text: The product P in the reaction,
19629.sol:
The reaction of a nitrile (R-CN$) with a Grignard reagent (R'-MgX$) followed by acidic hydrolysis (H_3O^{+}$) is a standard method for the synthesis of ketones.

The mechanism proceeds as follows:
1. The nucleophilic alkyl group (CH_3^{-}$) from the Grignard reagent attacks the electrophilic carbon of the nitrile group ($-CN$).
2. This forms an imine salt intermediate: $Ar-C(CH_3)=N-MgBr$.
3. Subsequent acidic hydrolysis (H_3O^{+}$) converts the imine intermediate into a ketone (Ar-C(=O)CH_3$) and releases ammonia/ammonium salts.

In the given substrate, 3-methoxybenzonitrile, the nitrile group is attached to the benzene ring at the meta position relative to the methoxy group. The reaction with $CH_3MgBr$ followed by $H_3O^{+}$ replaces the $-CN$ group with a $-COCH_3$ group.

Therefore, the product is 3-methoxyacetophenone, which corresponds to the structure with a benzene ring having a $-COCH_3$ group and a $-OCH_3$ group at the meta position.

19658.subject: Chemistry
19658.text: Which one of the following is the correct statement?
options: Fructose exists as a five membered ring named furanose.
Amylose is a water insoluble branched chain polymer of $\propto$-D-( - )-glucose.
Glucose gives Saccharic acid on reaction with $\mathrm{Br}_2$ water.
Cellulose is a branched chain polysaccharide having only $\propto$-D-glucose units.
19658.sol:
Fructose exists in a five-membered ring structure known as a furanose ring, which is formed by the intramolecular reaction between the carbonyl group at C-2 and the hydroxyl group at C-5. This statement is correct.

Amylose is a linear, water-soluble polymer of $\alpha$-D-glucose units, not a branched chain polymer. Amylopectin is the branched component of starch.

Glucose reacts with $\text{Br}_2$ water to form gluconic acid, which is a monocarboxylic acid. Saccharic acid (glucaric acid) is formed by the oxidation of glucose with stronger oxidizing agents like concentrated nitric acid, which oxidizes both the aldehyde group and the primary alcohol group.

Cellulose is a linear, unbranched polysaccharide consisting of $\beta$-D-glucose units linked by $\beta$-1,4-glycosidic bonds, not $\alpha$-D-glucose units.

Answer: Fructose exists as a five membered ring named furanose.

19858.subject: Chemistry
19858.text:
60% of a first order reaction was completed in 60 min, then 50% of the same reaction can be completed in:
[log 4 = 0.60, log 5=0.69]
19858.sol:
For a first order reaction, the rate constant $k$ is given by:

$k = \dfrac{2.303}{t} \log \left( \dfrac{a}{a-x} \right)

Given that 60\%$ of the reaction is completed in $60$ minutes:

$k = \dfrac{2.303}{60} \log \left( \dfrac{100}{100-60} \right)<$ br>
$k = \dfrac{2.303}{60} \log \left( \dfrac{100}{40} \right) = \dfrac{2.303}{60} \log (2.5)$

Using the given values, $\log (2.5) = \log \left( \dfrac{10}{4} \right) = \log10 - \log 4 = 1 - 0.60 = 0.40$

$k = \dfrac{2.303}{60} \times0.40$

The time required for $50\%$ completion (half-life) is:

$t_{50\%} = \dfrac{2.303}{k} \log \left( \dfrac{100}{100-50} \right) = \dfrac{2.303}{k} \log2$

Since $\log 4$ = 0.60$, we have 2 \log 2 = 0.60 \Rightarrow \log 2 = 0.30$

Substituting the value of $k$:

$t_{50\%} = \dfrac{2.303}{\dfrac{2.303}{60} \times 0.40} \times0.30$

$t_{50\%} = 60 \times \dfrac{0.30}{0.40} =60 \times \dfrac{3}{4} =45\ \text\min

Answer: 45\ \text\min$

20218.subject: Chemistry
20218.text: Lassaigne's test for the detection of nitrogen fails in
20218.sol:
Lassaigne's test for the detection of nitrogen involves the fusion of the organic compound with sodium metal to form sodium cyanide ($\text{NaCN}$).

For the formation of cyanide ion ($\text{CN}^{-}$), both carbon and nitrogen must be present in the organic compound.

Hydrazine hydrochloride ($\text{NH}_2\text{-NH}_2\cdot\text{HCl}$) does not contain carbon. Therefore, it cannot form sodium cyanide upon fusion with sodium metal, and Lassaigne's test for nitrogen fails.

The other compounds ($\text{NH}_2\text{CONH}_2$, $\text{NH}_2\text{CONHNH}_2\cdot\text{HCl}$, and $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NHNH}_2\cdot\text{HCl}$) contain both carbon and nitrogen, so they will give a positive test.

Answer: $\text{NH}_2\text{- NH}_2\text{HCl}$

21699.subject: Mathematics
21699.text: The maximum of $Z$ is where, $Z=4 x+2 y$ subject to constraints $4 x+2 y \geq 46, x+3 y \leq 24$ and $x, y \geq 0$ is
21699.sol:
The objective function is $Z = 4x + 2y$.

The constraints are:
1) $4x + 2y \geq 46 \Rightarrow 2x + y \geq 23$
2) $x + 3y \leq 24$
3) $x, y \geq 0$

We analyze the feasible region defined by these inequalities.
The line $2x + y = 23$ passes through $(11.5, 0)$ and $(0,23)$.
The line $x + 3y = 24$ passes through $(24,0)$ and $(0,8)$.

To find the intersection point of $2x + y = 23$ and $x + 3y = 24$:
From the first equation, $y = 23 - 2x$.
Substituting into the second: $x + 3(23 - 2x) = 24$
$x + 69 - 6x = 24$
$-5x = -45 \Rightarrow x = 9$
$y = 23 - 2(9) = 23 - 18 = 5$.
The intersection point is $(9,5)$.

Checking the constraints for the region $2x + y \geq 23$ and $x + 3y \leq 24$:
For $x=9, y=5$, $2(9) + 5 = 23$ (satisfied).
For $x=9, y=5$, $9 + 3(5) = 24$ (satisfied).
The region is bounded by the vertices $(11.5, 0)$, $(24,0)$, and $(9,5)$.

Evaluating $Z = 4x + 2y$ at the vertices:
At $(11.5, 0)$: $Z = 4(11.5) + 2(0) = 46$.
At $(24,0)$: $Z = 4(24) + 2(0) = 96$.
At $(9,5)$: $Z = 4(9) + 2(5) = 36 + 10 = 46$.

The maximum value of $Z$ in the feasible region is 96.

Answer: 96

22096.subject: Mathematics
22096.text: A line L passes through the point of intersection of the lines $3x + y - 10 = 0$ and $x - y - 2 = 0$. If the perpendicular distance of the line L from the point $(5, 1)$ is exactly $\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}}$ units, which of the following represents the correct equation for line L?
22096.sol:
The point of intersection of the lines $3x + y - 10 = 0$ and $x - y - 2 = 0$ is obtained by solving the two equations.

Adding the equations gives $4x - 12 = 0 \Rightarrow x = 3$.

Substituting $x = 3$ into $x - y - 2 = 0$ gives $y = 1$. Thus, the point of intersection is $(3, 1)$.

Let the equation of the required line L passing through $(3, 1)$ be $y - 1 = m(x - 3)$, which can be rewritten as $mx - y - 3m + 1 = 0$.

The perpendicular distance of line L from the point $(5, 1)$ is given as $\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}}$. Using the perpendicular distance formula:

$\dfrac{|m(5) - 1 - 3m + 1|}{\sqrt{m^2 + (-1)^2}} = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}}$

$\dfrac{|2m|}{\sqrt{m^2 + 1}} = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}}$

Squaring both sides:

$\dfrac{4m^2}{m^2 + 1} = \dfrac{4}{5}$

$5m^2 = m^2 + 1$

$4m^2 = 1 \Rightarrow m = \pm \dfrac{1}{2}$

For $m = \dfrac{1}{2}$, the equation of the line is $y - 1 = \dfrac{1}{2}(x - 3) \Rightarrow x - 2y - 1 = 0$.

For $m = -\dfrac{1}{2}$, the equation of the line is $y - 1 = -\dfrac{1}{2}(x - 3) \Rightarrow x + 2y - 5 = 0$.

Among the given options, $x + 2y - 5 = 0$ is the correct equation.

Answer: $x + 2y - 5 = 0$

22618.subject: Physics
22618.text: Two cells with the same emf $E$ and different internal resistances $r_1$ and $r_2$ are connected in series to an external resistance $R$. If the potential difference across the first cell is zero then value of $R$.
22618.sol:
The total emf of the two cells connected in series is $E_{total} = E + E = 2E$.

The total resistance of the circuit is $R_{total} = R + r_1 + r_2$.

The current $I$ flowing through the circuit is given by $I = \dfrac{2E}{R + r_1 + r_2}$.

The potential difference $V_1$ across the first cell is given by $V_1 = E - I r_1$.

Given that the potential difference across the first cell is zero, we set $V_1 = 0$, which implies $E = I r_1$.

Substituting the expression for $I$ into this equation, we get $E = \left( \dfrac{2E}{R + r_1 + r_2} \right) r_1$.

Dividing both sides by $E$, we obtain $1 = \dfrac{2r_1}{R + r_1 + r_2}$.

Rearranging the terms gives $R + r_1 + r_2 = 2r_1$.

Solving for $R$, we find $R = 2r_1 - r_1 - r_2 = r_1 - r_2$.

Answer: $r_1-r_2$

23327.subject: Physics
23327.text:
Two spring of force constant $k_{1}$ and $k_{2}$ are configured as the figure given below

The angular frequency of this configuration is
23327.sol:
In the given configuration, the block of mass $m$ is connected to two springs with force constants $k_{1}$ and $k_{2}$ on either side. When the block is displaced by a small distance $x$ from its equilibrium position, one spring is compressed by $x$ and the other is stretched by $x$.

The restoring force exerted by the first spring is $F_{1} = -k_{1}x$ and the restoring force exerted by the second spring is $F_{2} = -k_{2}x$. Both forces act in the same direction, opposing the displacement.

The total restoring force $F$ acting on the block is $F = F_{1} + F_{2} = -(k_{1} + k_{2})x$.

This is the standard form of the equation for simple harmonic motion, $F = -kx_{eff}$, where the effective spring constant $k_{eff} = k_{1} + k_{2}$.

The angular frequency $\omega$ of a mass-spring system is given by $\omega = \sqrt{\dfrac{k_{eff}}{m}}$.

Substituting the value of $k_{eff}$, we get $\omega = \sqrt{\dfrac{k_{1} + k_{2}}{m}}$.

Answer: $\sqrt{\dfrac{k_{1}+k_{2}}{m}}$

23357.subject: Physics
23357.text: A symmetric double convex lens is cut into two equal parts by a plane perpendicular to the principal axis. If the power of the original lens is 4D, the difference between the powers of the original lens and the cut lens is
23357.sol:
The power $P$ of a thin lens is given by the lens maker formula $P = (\mu - 1) \left( \dfrac{1}{R_1} - \dfrac{1}{R_2} \right)$. For a symmetric double convex lens, $R_1 = R$ and $R_2 = -R$.

Thus, $P = (\mu - 1) \left( \dfrac{1}{R} - \dfrac{1}{-R} \right) = (\mu - 1) \dfrac{2}{R} = 4$ D.

When the lens is cut into two equal parts by a plane perpendicular to the principal axis, each part becomes a plano-convex lens. For a plano-convex lens, one surface has radius $R$ and the other is flat, meaning $R_1 = R$ and $R_2 = \infty$.

The power of each cut lens $P'$ is $P' = (\mu - 1) \left( \dfrac{1}{R} - \dfrac{1}{\infty} \right) = \dfrac{\mu - 1}{R}$.

Comparing $P$ and $P'$, we see that $P' = \dfrac{1}{2} P$.

Given $P = 4$ D, the power of each cut lens is $P' = \dfrac{4}{2} = 2$ D.

The difference between the power of the original lens and the cut lens is $P - P' = 4 - 2 = 2$ D.

Answer: 2 D

$\left(I\right)$ $f\left(x\right) = sin ⁡ \left(\picos ⁡ x\right)$ and $X = \left\{x: f\left(x\right) = 0\right\}$
$f\left(x\right) = 0$
$⇒ sin ⁡ \left(\picos ⁡ x\right) = 0$
$⇒ \picos ⁡ x = m\pi, m \in I$
$⇒ cos ⁡ x = m$
$cos ⁡ x = 0, 1, - 1$
$⇒ x = \dfrac{n\pi}{2}$
$⇒ X = \left\{\dfrac{n\pi}{2}, n \in I\right\} ⇒ X = \left\{\pm \dfrac{\pi}{2}, \pm \pi, \pm \dfrac{3\pi}{2}, \pm 2\pi \ldots \ldots\right\}$

$⇒ 2\pisin ⁡ x = \left(2m + 1\right)\dfrac{\pi}{2}, m \in I$
$⇒ sin ⁡ x = \dfrac{2n + 1}{4}$
$⇒ sin ⁡ x = - \dfrac{1}{4}, \dfrac{1}{4}, \dfrac{- 3}{4}, \dfrac{3}{4}$
$⇒ Z = \left\{n\pi \pm \sin^{- 1} ⁡ \left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right), n\pi \pm \sin^{- 1} ⁡ \left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right)\right\}, n \in I$

or $sin ⁡ x = 0 ⇒ x = n\pi$
Hence, $Y = \left\{n\pi, n\pi \pm \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right\}, n \in I$
$Y = \left\{\dfrac{\pi}{3}, \dfrac{2\pi}{3}, \pi, \dfrac{4\pi}{3}, \dfrac{5\pi}{3}, 2\pi \ldots\right\}$
$\left(III\right) \to R$

or $sin ⁡ \left(2\pisin ⁡ x\right) = 0$

$⇒ sin ⁡ x = - 1, - \dfrac{1}{2}, 0, \dfrac{1}{2}, 1$
$⇒ x = \dfrac{n\pi}{2}, n\pi \pm \dfrac{\pi}{6}, n \in I$

26010.text:
In a circuit, a metal filament lamp is connected in series with a capacitor of capacitance $\mathrm{C} \mu F$ across a $200 \mathrm{~V}, 50 \mathrm{~Hz}$ supply. The power consumed by the lamp is $500 \mathrm{~W}$ while the voltage drop across it is $100 \mathrm{~V}$. Assume that there is no inductive load in the circuit. Take $r m s$ values of the voltages. The magnitude of the phaseangle (in degrees) between the current and the supply voltage is $\varphi$. Assume, $\pi \sqrt{3} \approx 5$.
The value of $C$ is ____.
26010.sol:
Given,

$P = 500W$

${V}_{R} = 100V$

$f = 50Hz$

${V}_{rms} = 200V$

$P = \dfrac{{{V}_{R}}^{2}}{R} ⇒ R = \dfrac{{{V}_{R}}^{2}}{P} ⇒ R = \dfrac{{\left(100\right)}^{2}}{500}$

$∴ R = 20Ω$

Now current in the circuit,

$i = {i}_{rms} = \dfrac{voltageacrossresistor}{resistance}i = \dfrac{100}{20}i = 5A$

Phasor diagram of the given circuit for voltage,

Now,

${V}^{2} = {{V}_{C}}^{2} + {{V}_{R}}^{2} ⇒ {200}^{2} = {{V}_{C}}^{2} + {100}^{2} ⇒ {V}_{C} = 100\sqrt{3}V$

Now,

${V}_{C} = 100\sqrt{3}V = I{X}_{C} ⇒ {X}_{C} = \dfrac{100\sqrt{3}}{5} = 20\sqrt{3}Ω$

and

${X}_{C} = \dfrac{1}{\left(2\pif\right)C} ⇒ 20\sqrt{3} = \dfrac{1}{\left(2\pi \times 100\right)C} ⇒ C = 100\mu F$

From the phasor diagram,

$tan\left(ϕ\right) = \dfrac{{X}_{C}}{R} = \dfrac{20\sqrt{3}}{20} = \sqrt{3} ⇒ ϕ = 60 °$

29024.subject: Chemistry
29024.text:
The correct order of first $(\Delta_i H_1)$ and second $(\Delta_i H_2)$ ionisation enthalpy values of Cr and Mn are :
A. $\Delta_i H_1 :$ Cr $>$ Mn
B. $\Delta_i H_2 :$ Cr $>$ Mn
C. $\Delta_i H_1 :$ Mn $>$ Cr
D. $\Delta_i H_2 :$ Mn $>$ Cr
Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
29024.sol:
The electronic configuration of Cr is $[Ar] 3d^5 4s^1$ and Mn is $[Ar] 3d^5 4s^2$.

For the first ionization enthalpy, the electron is removed from the $4s$ orbital. Mn has a fully filled $4s^2$ configuration and a higher effective nuclear charge compared to Cr. Thus, the first ionization enthalpy of Mn is greater than that of Cr ($\Delta_i H_1 :$ Mn $>$ Cr). This makes statement C correct.

After the first ionization, the electronic configurations become:
$Cr^+ : [Ar] 3d^5$
$Mn^+ : [Ar] 3d^5 4s^1$

For the second ionization enthalpy, the electron is removed from the highly stable half-filled $3d^5$ subshell in $Cr^+$, whereas in $Mn^+$, it is removed from the $4s^1$ orbital. Removing an electron from a stable half-filled configuration requires significantly more energy. Thus, the second ionization enthalpy of Cr is greater than that of Mn ($\Delta_i H_2 :$ Cr $>$ Mn). This makes statement B correct.

Therefore, the correct statements are B and C.

Answer: B and C only

33551.subject: Mathematics
33551.text: Let a circle pass through the origin and its centre be the point of intersection of two mutually perpendicular lines $x + (k-1)y + 3 = 0$ and $2x + k^2 y - 4 = 0$. If the line $x - y + 2 = 0$ intersects the circle at the points A and B, then $(AB)^2$ is equal to:
33551.sol:
The given lines are $x + (k-1)y + 3 = 0 and 2x + k^2 y - 4 = 0$.

Since they are mutually perpendicular, the product of their slopes is $-1$:

$\left(\dfrac{-1}{k-1}\right) \left(\dfrac{-2}{k^2}\right) = -1$

$\dfrac{2}{k^2(k-1)} = -1 \Rightarrow k^3 - k^2 + 2 = 0$

By trial, $k = -1$ is a root. Factoring gives $(k+1)(k^2 - 2k + 2) = 0$. Since $k^2 - 2k + 2 = 0$ has no real roots, $k = -1$.

Substituting $k = -1$ into the equations of the lines, we get:

$x - 2y + 3 = 0$

$2x + y - 4 = 0$

Solving these two equations, we get the point of intersection as $x = 1 and y = 2$. Thus, the centre of the circle is $C(1, 2)$.

Since the circle passes through the origin $(0,0)$, the square of its radius $R$ is:

$R^2 = (1 - 0)^2 + (2 - 0)^2 = 5$

The perpendicular distance $d$ from the centre $C(1, 2)$ to the line $x - y + 2 = 0$ is:

$d = \dfrac{|1 - 2 + 2|}{\sqrt{1^2 + (-1)^2}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$

The length of the chord $AB$ is given by $2\sqrt{R^2 - d^2}$. Therefore, its square is:

$(AB)^2 = 4(R^2 - d^2) = 4\left(5 - \dfrac{1}{2}\right) = 4 \times \dfrac{9}{2} = 18$

Answer: $18$

35029.text: Let $E$ be an ellipse whose axes are parallel to the co-ordinates axes, having its centre at $\left(3, - 4\right),$ one focus at $\left(4, - 4\right)$ and one vertex at $\left(5, - 4\right) .$ If $mx - y = 4, m > 0$ is a tangent to the ellipse $E,$ then the value of $5{m}^{2}$ is equal to _____ .
35029.sol:
We know that, If the standard ellipse is shifted to have center $\left(h, k\right)$, then it's equation is $\dfrac{{\left(x - h\right)}^{2}}{{a}^{2}} + \dfrac{{\left(y - k\right)}^{2}}{{b}^{2}} = 1$

The center is $C\left(h, k\right)$
The vertices on the major axis are $A\left(h + a, k\right)$ and ${A}^{'}\left(h - a, k\right)$
The foci are $S\left(h + ae, k\right)$ and ${S}^{'}\left(h - ae, k\right)$

The eccentricity $e = \sqrt{\dfrac{{a}^{2} - {b}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}}$

Given $C\left(3, - 4\right), S\left(4, - 4\right)$ and $A\left(5, - 4\right)$

Therefore, $\left(h, k\right) = \left(3, - 4\right)$

$\left(h + a, k\right) = \left(5, - 4\right)$

$\left(h + ae, k\right) = \left(4, - 4\right)$

Clearly, $a = 2 \text{ and } ae = 1$

$⇒ e = \dfrac{1}{2}$

We know that, ${b}^{2} = {a}^{2}\left(1 - {e}^{2}\right)$

${b}^{2} = {a}^{2} - {a}^{2}{e}^{2}$

${b}^{2} = {2}^{2} - 1$

$⇒ {b}^{2} = 3$

So, equation of ellipse $\dfrac{{\left(x - 3\right)}^{2}}{4} + \dfrac{{\left(y + 4\right)}^{2}}{3} = 1$

Intersecting with given tangent

$\dfrac{{x}^{2} - 6x + 9}{4} + \dfrac{{m}^{2}{x}^{2}}{3} = 1$

$⇒ 3\left({x}^{2} - 6x + 9\right) + 4{m}^{2}{x}^{2} = 12$

$⇒ 3{x}^{2} - 18x + 27 + 4{m}^{2}{x}^{2} = 12$

$⇒ \left(3 + 4{m}^{2}\right){x}^{2} - 18x + 15 = 0$

Now, $D = 0$ (as it is tangent)

$⇒ {\left(18\right)}^{2} = 4\left(3 + 4{m}^{2}\right) \times 15$

So, $5{m}^{2} = 3 .$

$⇒ \lim_{x \to 0}\dfrac{( 3 + \beta ) + ( \alpha - 1 ) x + \left(- \dfrac{1}{2} - \dfrac{\beta}{2}\right){x}^{2} + \ldots .}{3{x}^{2}} \times \dfrac{{x}^{2}}{\tan^{2}x} = \dfrac{1}{3}$

The coefficient of all the powers of $x$ except ${x}^{2}$ is $0$.

$⇒ \beta + 3 = 0, \alpha - 1 = 0$ and $\dfrac{- \dfrac{1}{2} - \dfrac{\beta}{2}}{3} = \dfrac{1}{3}$

$⇒ \beta = - 3, \alpha = 1$

$⇒ 2\alpha - \beta = 2 + 3 = 5$

$∴ 3{a}^{2} + 4{b}^{2} = 4$

37032.sol:
Evaluate $\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} (-1)^{k+1} \frac{k(k+1)}{k!}$.
Rewrite as $\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} (-1)^{k+1} \frac{k+1}{(k-1)!}$ and split: $\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} (-1)^{k+1} \frac{k}{(k-1)!} + \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} (-1)^{k+1} \frac{1}{(k-1)!}$.
The first sum, after rewriting $\frac{k}{(k-1)!} = \frac{1}{(k-2)!} + \frac{1}{(k-1)!}$ for $k \geq 2$, evaluates to 0 using the exponential series $\sum_{j=0}^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^j}{j!} = e^{-1}$.
The second sum with substitution $j = k-1$ gives $\sum_{j=0}^{\infty} (-1)^j \frac{1}{j!} = e^{-1} = \frac{1}{e}$.
Therefore, the total is $0 + \frac{1}{e} = \frac{1}{e}$.

General term of the given series is given by,

${T}_{n} = \dfrac{n}{1 - 3{n}^{2} + {n}^{4}}$

$⇒ {T}_{n} = \dfrac{n}{\left({n}^{4} - 2{n}^{2} + 1\right) - {n}^{2}}$

$⇒ {T}_{n} = \dfrac{1}{2}\left[\dfrac{1}{\left({n}^{2} - 1 - n\right)} - \dfrac{1}{\left({n}^{2} - 1 + n\right)}\right]$

$⇒ \mathop{∑}_{n = 1}^{10}{T}_{n} = \dfrac{1}{2}\left[\left(\dfrac{1}{- 1} - \dfrac{1}{1}\right) + \left(\dfrac{1}{1} - \dfrac{1}{5}\right) + \left(\dfrac{1}{5} - \dfrac{1}{11}\right) + . . . + \left(\dfrac{1}{89} - \dfrac{1}{109}\right)\right]$

$⇒ \mathop{∑}_{n = 1}^{10}{T}_{n} = \dfrac{1}{2}\left[- 1 - \dfrac{1}{109}\right]$

$⇒ \mathop{∑}_{n = 1}^{10}{T}_{n} = \dfrac{- 55}{109}$

Whose normal vector is $≡ \overset{¯}{n}1 = \left(2, - 2, 1\right)

Whose normal vector is $≡ \overset{¯}{n}2 = $\left(1, - 1, 2\right)$

Now let plane perpendicular to ${P}_{1} and {P}_{2}$ will have normal vector $\overset{¯}{n}3$

$⇒ \overset{\to}{n}3 = $\left|\begin{cases}\overset{^}{i} & \overset{^}{j} & \overset{^}{k} \\ 2 & - 2 & 1 \\ 1 & - 1 & 2\end{cases}\right|$ = - 3\overset{^}{i} - 3\overset{^}{j}$

Hence, $\overset{¯}{n}3 = $\left(- 3, - 3, 0\right)$

Equation of plane $E$ through $P\left(1, - 1, 1\right) and $\overset{¯}{n}3$ as normal vector will be,$

$- 3 \left(x - 1\right) - 3 \left(y + 1\right) + 0 \left(z - 1\right) = 0$

In two different experiments, an object of mass $5kg$ moving with a speed of $25{ms}^{- 1}$ hits two different walls and comes to rest within

Average force will be same for both the cases but the impulse will be different.
Average force and impulse will be different for both the cases.
39309.sol:
Impulse $=$ Change in momentum

$I = \DeltaP$

Therefore, in both the cases the impulse is same.

Average force is defined as,

${F}_{avg} = \dfrac{\DeltaP}{\Deltat}$

Since the time in the two cases is different, the average force will be different.

41951.text: Eight equal drops of water are falling through air with a steady speed of $10cm{s}^{- 1}$. If the drops coalesce, the new velocity is:-

The terminal velocity can be given by

${v}_{T} = \dfrac{2 ( ρ - \sigma ) {r}^{2}g}{9η}$.

Clearly, ${v}_{T} ∝ {r}^{2}$

Let the radius of the small drops be ${r}_{1}$ and the radius of the big drop be ${r}_{2}$.

So,

$8\left(\dfrac{4\pi}{3}\right){r}_{1}^{3} = \left(\dfrac{4\pi}{3}\right){r}_{2}^{3} ⇒ {r}_{1} = \dfrac{{r}_{2}}{2}$

Hence, taking the ratio
$\dfrac{{\left({v}_{T}\right)}_{1}}{{\left({v}_{T}\right)}_{2}} = {\left(\dfrac{{r}_{1}}{{r}_{2}}\right)}^{2}$
$⇒ \dfrac{10}{{\left({v}_{T}\right)}_{2}} = \dfrac{1}{4}$

42234.text: Form the $v - t$ graph shown, the ratio of distance to displacement in $25s$ of motion is:
42234.sol:
The area under the velocity time graph gives the displacement. The area for $t = 0s\text{to}t = 25s$is

$( Area ) = \left(\dfrac{1}{2} \times 5 \times 10\right) + \left(5 \times 10\right) + \left(\dfrac{1}{2} \times 30 \times 5\right) + \left(\dfrac{1}{2} \times 20 \times 5\right) - \left(\dfrac{1}{2} \times 20 \times 5\right)$

$⇒ Area = 25 + 50 + 75 + 50 - 50 = 150m$
Hence, the displacement $= 150m$

The distance is defined as the path taken by the object to travel from initial to final position. Also note that displacement is a vector quantity, but distance is a scalar quantity.
Distance $= \left(\dfrac{1}{2} \times 5 \times 10\right) + \left(5 \times 10\right) + \left(\dfrac{1}{2} \times 30 \times 5\right) + \left(\dfrac{1}{2} \times 20 \times 5\right) + \left(\dfrac{1}{2} \times 20 \times 5\right) = ( 200 + 50 ) = 250m$

Therefore, required ratio
$\dfrac{\text{distance}}{\text{displacement}} = \dfrac{250}{150} = \left(\dfrac{5}{3}\right)$

46582.text:
Two rigid bodies $A and B$ rotate with rotational kinetic energies $E_A and E_B$ respectively. The moments of inertia of $A and B$ about the axis of rotation are $I_A and I_B$ respectively.
If $I_A=\frac{I_B}{4}$ and E_A=100=E_B, the ratio of angular momentum $\left(L_A\right)$ of A to the angular momentum $\left(L_B\right)$ of B is
46582.sol:
From, the formula, rotational KE
$E_{\text{rotational }}=\frac{1}{2} l \omega^2=\frac{L^2}{2 \mid}(\because L=\mid \omega)$
Therefore, $\quad L^2=2 E l$
Hence
$L_A^2=2 E_A I_A\ldots(i)$ and $L_B^2=2 E_B I_B\ldots(ii)$
From Eq. (i) and (ii)
$\begin{aligned} & \frac{L_A}{L_B}=\sqrt{\frac{2 E_A I_B}{2 E_B I_A}}=\sqrt{\frac{100}{4}}=5 \\ & \quad\left(\because \frac{E_B}{E_A}=100 \text{$ and $} \frac{I_A}{I_B}=4\right)\end{aligned}$

49912.text: A copper wire of length $1 \mathrm{ m}$ and uniform cross-sectional area $5 \times 10^{-7} \mathrm{ m}^{2}$ carries a current of $1 \mathrm{ A}$. Assuming that, there are $8 \times 10^{28}$ free electrons per $\mathrmm^{3}$ in copper, how long will an electron take to drift from one end of the wire to the other?
49912.sol:
Given, $l=1 \mathrm{ m}\begin{aligned}
&A=5 \times 10^{-7} \mathrm{ m}^{2} \\
&I=1 \mathrm{ A} \\
&n=8 \times 10^{28} \text{ electrons } / \mathrm{m}^{3}
\end{aligned}$
Time taken by an electron to take the drift from one end to the other is given as
$T=\frac{l}{v_{d}}...(i)$
where, $v_{d}$ is the drift velocity.
As, $v_{d}=\frac{I}{n e A}=\frac{1}{8 \times 10^{28} \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 5 \times 10^{-7}}=\frac{1}{6.4 \times 10^{3}}$
So, substituting the given values in Eq. (i), we get
$T=\frac{1}{\frac{1}{6.4 \times 10^{3}}}=6.4 \times 10^{3} \mathrm{ s}$

50136.subject: Physics
50136.text: A point charge $q$ is placed at the corner of a cube of side $a$ as shown in the figure. What is the electric flux through the face $A B C D$ ?
50136.sol:
If charge is placed at the one corner of a cube, then it can be shared further by 8 cubes.
$\therefore$ Charge on one cube $=\frac{q}{8}$
Now, in any given cube this charge will be touching 3 out of 9 of cube faces. So, the area vector of that side and the electric field vector will be perpendicular. So, flux through those 3 sides will be zero. However, equal amount of flux will flow from other 3 sides.
So, flux through one side $=\left(\frac{q / 8}{3}\right) \cdot \frac{1}{\varepsilon_{0}}=\frac{q}{24 \varepsilon_{0}}$ Hence, flux through one face $(A B C D)=\frac{q}{24 \varepsilon_{0}}$

53289.text: If an edge of a cube measure 2 m with a possible error of 0.5 cm. Find the corresponding error in the calculated volume of the cube
53289.sol:
Let $x$ be the length of an edge of a cube and $V$ be the volume of that cube. $V=x^3$ On differentiating w.r.t. $x$, we get $\frac{d V}{d x}=3 x^2$ Let $\delta V$ be error in $V$ and corresponding error $\delta x in x$. $\therefore \quad \delta V=\frac{d V}{d x} \delta x=3 x^2 \delta x$
Given that, $x=2 \mathrm{ m}$ and $\delta x=0.5 \mathrm{ cm}=\frac{0.5}{100} \mathrm{ m}\begin{aligned} \therefore \quad \delta V & =3(2)^2\left(\frac{0.5}{100}\right) \\ & =\frac{12 \times 0.5}{100}=\frac{6}{100}=0.06 \mathrm{ m}^3 \end{aligned}$

57607.text: Which of the following has highest reactivity towards nucleophilic substitution reaction involving cleavage of $\mathrm{C}-\mathrm{Cl}$ bond?
57607.sol:
Electron-withdrawing groups at ortho and para positions enhance nucleophilic aromatic substitution by stabilizing the Meisenheimer complex through resonance.

Chlorobenzene lacks electron-withdrawing groups and shows minimal reactivity.

p-Nitrochlorobenzene has one nitro group at the para position, providing moderate stabilization.

2,4-Dinitrochlorobenzene features nitro groups at ortho and para positions, offering greater stabilization.

2,4,6-Trinitrochlorobenzene possesses three nitro groups at ortho and para positions, delivering maximum stabilization and thus the highest reactivity.

The reactivity order is chlorobenzene $\ll$ p-nitrochlorobenzene < 2,4-dinitrochlorobenzene < 2,4,6-trinitrochlorobenzene.

58012.subject: Chemistry
58012.text:
A monobasic weak acid dissociates $2 \%$ in its 0.002 M solution.
Calculate the dissociation constant of weak acid.
58012.sol:
Dissociation constant calculation for weak acids

For a weak acid HA with dissociation equilibrium $\text{HA} \rightleftharpoons \text{H}^+ + \text{A}^-$, the acid dissociation constant is given by $K_a = \frac{[\text{H}^+][\text{A}^-]}{[\text{HA}]}$.

Given initial concentration $C = 0.002\ \text{M}$ and percentage dissociation 2%, the degree of dissociation is $\alpha = 0.02$.

From the equilibrium concentrations $[\text{H}^+] = [\text{A}^-] = C\alpha$ and $[\text{HA}] = C(1-\alpha)$, the dissociation constant becomes $K_a = \frac{C\alpha^2}{1-\alpha}$.

Since $\alpha = 0.02$ is sufficiently small, we apply the approximation $1-\alpha \approx 1$, yielding $K_a \approx C\alpha^2$.

Substituting values: $K_a \approx (2 \times 10^{-3}) \times (2 \times 10^{-2})^2 = 8 \times 10^{-7}$.

The calculated value matches option B.

59110.text: For a binary solution, when a nonvolatile nonelectrolyte solute is dissolved in solvent, the vapour pressure of solvent decreases by 20 %. what is mole fraction of solvent in solution ?
59110.sol:
Let the vapour pressure of the pure solvent be $P^0$.

The decrease in vapour pressure is given as $20\%$, so the lowering of vapour pressure is $\Delta P = 0.20 P^0$.

According to Raoult's law, the relative lowering of vapour pressure is equal to the mole fraction of the solute, $X_{\text{solute}}$.

$\dfrac{\Delta P}{P^0} = X_{\text{solute}}$

$X_{\text{solute}} = \dfrac{0.20 P^0}{P^0} = 0.20$

For a binary solution, the sum of mole fractions of solute and solvent is $1$.

$X_{\text{solvent}} = 1 - X_{\text{solute}}$

$X_{\text{solvent}} = 1 - 0.20 = 0.8$

Answer: $0.8$

59174.subject: Chemistry
59174.text:
Find molar mass of nonvolatile solute when 20 g of it dissolved in 200 g
water at 300 K.
[Relative lowering of vapour pressure $=0.02$ ]
59174.sol:
The molar mass of a nonvolatile solute dissolved in a solvent can be determined from the relative lowering of vapor pressure using Raoult's law.

For a dilute solution, the relative lowering of vapor pressure is approximately equal to the mole fraction of the solute: $\frac{P^0 - P_s}{P^0} \approx \frac{n_2}{n_1}$, where $n_1$ and $n_2$ represent the number of moles of solvent and solute, respectively.

Given $\frac{P^0 - P_s}{P^0} = 0.02$ with 20 g of solute in 200 g of water (molar mass 18 g/mol), the moles of solvent are $n_1 = \frac{200}{18} = \frac{100}{9}$.

Substituting into the relation gives $0.02 = \frac{20 / M_2}{200 / 18} = \frac{360}{200 M_2}$.

Solving for $M_2$ yields $M_2 = \frac{360}{200 \times 0.02} = \frac{360}{4} = 90$ g/mol.

Final answer: $\boxed{90}$ g mol^{-1}$

$

59941.text:
Calculate work done if 1 mole of an ideal gas compressed isothermally and reversibly from $12 \mathrm{dm}^3$ to $6 \mathrm{dm}^3$ at 300 K .
$\left[\mathrm{R}=8 \cdot 314 \mathrm{JK}^{-1} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}\right]$
59941.sol:
For an ideal gas undergoing isothermal reversible compression, the work done is given by $W = -nRT \ln \left(\frac{V_2}{V_1}\right).

Substituting $n = 1 $\text{mol}, $R = 8.314 $\text{J K}^{-1} \text{mol}^{-1},$ and T = 300 $\text{K},$ with V_1 = 12 $\text{dm}^$3$, $V_2 = 6 $\text{dm}^$3$, the expression becomes $W = -(1)(8.314)(300) \ln $\left(\frac{6}{12}\right)$.

Evaluating the numerical coefficient yields $-2494.2 \text{J}$. Since $\ln(0.5) \approx -0.6931$, the work done is $W = -2494.2 \times (-0.6931) \approx 1728.8 \text{J}$.

Converting to kilojoules, $W \approx 1.7288 \text{kJ}$, which rounds to $1.729 \text{kJ}$ to three decimal places.

The work done is positive, consistent with compression, and matches option A.

62826.subject: Mathematics
62826.text: The point at which the maximum value of $x + y$ subject to constraints $x + 2y \leq 70$ and $2x + y \leq 95, x \geq 0, y \geq 0$ is.
62826.sol:
The objective function to be maximized is $Z = x + y$.

The given constraints are:
$x + 2y \leq 70$
$2x + y \leq 95$
$x \geq 0, y \geq 0$

The corner points of the feasible region are determined by the intersections of the boundary lines $x + 2y = 70$, $2x + y = 95$, and the coordinate axes.

Solving $x + 2y = 70$ and $2x + y = 95$:
Multiplying the second equation by $2$ gives $4x + 2y = 190$.
Subtracting the first equation from this gives $3x = 120 \Rightarrow x = 40$.
Substituting $x = 40$ into $x + 2y = 70$ gives $40 + 2y = 70 \Rightarrow 2y = 30 \Rightarrow y = 15$.
The intersection point is $(40,15)$.

The corner points of the bounded feasible region are $(0,0)$, $(47.5, 0)$, $(40,15)$, and $(0,35)$.

Evaluating $Z = x + y$ at each corner point:
At $(0,0)$, $Z = 0 + 0 = 0$
At $(47.5, 0)$, $Z = 47.5 + 0 = 47.5$
At $(40,15)$, $Z = 40 + 15 = 55$
At $(0,35)$, $Z = 0 + 35 = 35$

The maximum value of $Z$ is $55$, which occurs at the point $(40,15)$.

Answer: $(40,15)$

63154.subject: Mathematics
63154.text: $The inverse of matrix \begin{bmatrix} 1+pq & p & 0 \\ q & 1+pq & p \\ 0 & q & 1 \end{bmatrix}$ is...
options: $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & p & p^2 \\ q & 1+pq & p+p^2q \\ q^2 & q+pq^2 & 1+pq+p^2q^2 \end{bmatrix}$
63154.sol:
Let the given matrix be $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1+pq & p & 0 \\ q & 1+pq & p \\ 0 & q & 1 \end{bmatrix}$.

The inverse of matrix $A$ is given by $A^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{|A|}\text{adj}(A)$.

First, evaluate the determinant of $A$:

$|A| = (1+pq)[(1+pq)(1) - (p)(q)] - p[q(1) - (p)(0)] + 0$

$|A| = (1+pq)[1 + pq - pq] - p[q]$

$|A| = (1+pq)(1) - pq = 1 + pq - pq = 1$

Since $|A| = 1$, the inverse matrix is $A^{-1} = \text{adj}(A)$.

To find the adjoint of $A$, we calculate the cofactors of each element:

$C_{11} = (1+pq)(1) - pq = 1$

$C_{12} = -(q(1) - 0) = -q$

$C_{13} = q(q) - 0 = q^2$

$C_{21} = -(p(1) - 0) = -p$

$C_{22} = (1+pq)(1) - 0 = 1+pq$

$C_{23} = -((1+pq)q - 0) = -(q + pq^2)$

$C_{31} = p(p) - 0 = p^2$

$C_{32} = -((1+pq)p - 0) = -(p + p^2q)$

$C_{33} = (1+pq)^2 - pq = 1 + 2pq + p^2q^2 - pq = 1 + pq + p^2q^2$

The adjoint matrix is the transpose of the cofactor matrix:

$\text{adj}(A) = \begin{bmatrix} C_{11} & C_{21} & C_{31} \\ C_{12} & C_{22} & C_{32} \\ C_{13} & C_{23} & C_{33} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -p & p^2 \\ -q & 1+pq & -(p+p^2q) \\ q^2 & -(q+pq^2) & 1+pq+p^2q^2 \end{bmatrix}$

Therefore, $A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -p & p^2 \\ -q & 1+pq & -(p+p^2q) \\ q^2 & -(q+pq^2) & 1+pq+p^2q^2 \end{bmatrix}$.

63967.subject: Mathematics
63967.text:
If $p_1, p_2, p_3$ are altitudes of a triangle $A B C$ from the vertices $A, B, C$ respectively and if $\Delta$ is the area of the triangle, $S$ is the semi perimeter of the triangle, then
$\frac{\operatorname{Cos} \mathrm{A}}{\mathrm{p}_1}+\frac{\operatorname{Cos} \mathrm{B}}{\mathrm{p}_2}+\frac{\operatorname{Cos} \mathrm{C}}{\mathrm{p}_3}$
63967.sol:
The area $\Delta$ of a triangle can be expressed in terms of its altitudes $p_1$, $p_2$, $p_3$ and corresponding sides as $\Delta = \frac{1}{2} a p_1 = \frac{1}{2} b p_2 = \frac{1}{2} c p_3$.

Solving for the altitudes gives $p_1 = \frac{2\Delta}{a}$, $p_2 = \frac{2\Delta}{b}$, and $p_3 = \frac{2\Delta}{c}$.

Substituting into the expression $E = \frac{\cos A}{p_1} + \frac{\cos B}{p_2} + \frac{\cos C}{p_3}$ yields:
$E = \frac{\cos A}{\frac{2\Delta}{a}} + \frac{\cos B}{\frac{2\Delta}{b}} + \frac{\cos C}{\frac{2\Delta}{c}} = \frac{1}{2\Delta}(a\cos A + b\cos B + c\cos C)$.

Using the law of sines, $a = 2R\sin A$, $b = 2R\sin B$, and $c = 2R\sin C$, the expression becomes:
$a\cos A + b\cos B + c\cos C = 2R(\sin A\cos A + \sin B\cos B + \sin C\cos C)$.

Applying the identity $\sin2x = 2\sin x\cos x$ gives:
$2R(\sin A\cos A + \sin B\cos B + \sin C\cos C) = R(\sin2A + \sin2B + \sin2C)$.

Using the triangle identity $\sin2A + \sin2B + \sin2C = 4\sin A\sin B\sin C$, we obtain:
$a\cos A + b\cos B + c\cos C = 4R\sin A\sin B\sin C$.

Substituting back, $E = \frac{1}{2\Delta}(4R\sin A\sin B\sin C) = \frac{2R\sin A\sin B\sin C}{\Delta}$.

From the formula $\Delta = 2R^2\sin A\sin B\sin C$, we have $\sin A\sin B\sin C = \frac{\Delta}{2R^2}$, yielding:
$E = \frac{2R\cdot\frac{\Delta}{2R^2}}{\Delta} = \frac{1}{R}$.

64340.text: The Cartesian equations of the line passing through $A(0, 1, 1)$ and parallel to the X-axis are....
64340.sol:
The direction ratios of the X-axis are $1, 0, 0$.

The line passes through the point $A(0, 1, 1)$ and is parallel to the X-axis. Therefore, its direction ratios are $1, 0, 0$.

The Cartesian equations of the line are given by:

$\dfrac{x - 0}{1} = \dfrac{y - 1}{0} = \dfrac{z - 1}{0}$

This implies $y - 1 = 0$ and $z - 1 = 0$.

Thus, the equations of the line are $y = 1, z = 1$.

Answer: $y = 1, z = 1$

65147.subject: Mathematics
65147.text: In the above figure, P divides AC in the ratio 3:4 and Q divides BC in the ratio $4: 3$. Then $M$ divides $A Q$ in the ratio
65147.sol:
To determine the ratio in which $M$ divides $\overline{AQ}$, two approaches are presented.

Method 1: Menelaus' Theorem
Apply Menelaus' theorem to $\triangle ACQ$ with transversal $B-M-P$:

$\left(\frac{AP}{PC}\right) \cdot \left(\frac{CB}{BQ}\right) \cdot \left(\frac{QM}{MA}\right) = 1$

Given $AP:PC = 3:4 and BQ:QC = 4:3$, compute $\frac{CB}{BQ} = 1 + \frac{QC}{BQ} = \frac{7}{4}$. Substituting:

$\left(\frac{3}{4}\right) \cdot \left(\frac{7}{4}\right) \cdot \left(\frac{QM}{MA}\right) = 1$

$\frac{QM}{MA} = \frac{16}{21}$, hence $AM:MQ = 21:16$.

Method 2: Mass Point Geometry
Assign masses at $A$, $B$, $C$ using the given ratios. For $AP:PC = 3:4$, let $m_A = 4 and m_C = 3$. For $BQ:QC = 4:3$, let $m_B = 3 and m_C = 4$. To reconcile $m_C$, scale by $k=4 and j=3$: $m_A = 16$, $m_B = 9$, $m_C = 12$.

Since $M$ lies on $\overline{AQ}$ and is the centroid, $AM:MQ = m_Q:m_A = (m_B + m_C):m_A = 21:16$.

The ratio is $\boxed{21:16}$.

68493.subject: Physics
68493.text: A particle is performing U.C.M. along a circle of radius $R$. In half the period of revolution, its displacement and distance covered are respectively
68493.sol:
In half the period of revolution, the particle moves from its initial position to the diametrically opposite point on the circular path.

The displacement is the shortest distance between the initial and final positions, which is equal to the diameter of the circle.

Displacement = $2R$

The distance covered is the actual path length along the circular trajectory, which is half of the circumference.

Distance = $\dfrac{2\pi R}{2} = \pi R$

Answer: $2R, \pi R$

68702.text: A small sphere oscillates simple harmonically in a watch glass whose radius of curvature is 1.6 m. The period of oscillation of the sphere is (acceleration due to gravity $g=10 \mathrm{ m} / \mathrm{s}^2$ )
68702.sol:
The motion of a small sphere oscillating in a watch glass is equivalent to a simple pendulum’s motion, with the effective length equal to the watch glass’s radius of curvature.

The period of oscillation is given by $T = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{L}{g}}$, where $L = R = 1.6\mathrm{m}$ and $g = 10\mathrm{m/s^2}$.

Substituting these values yields $T = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{1.6}{10}} = 2\pi \sqrt{0.16} = 2\pi \times 0.4 = 0.8\pi\mathrm{s}$.

This result corresponds to option D.

71025.subject: Biology
71025.text: The approximate size of a nucleus in a typical mammalian cell is about ______ meter and the length of DNA molecule is about ______ meters respectively.
71025.sol:
The length of the DNA double helix in a typical mammalian cell is calculated by multiplying the total number of base pairs with the distance between two consecutive base pairs.

Length of DNA = $6.6 \times 10^{9} \times 0.34 \times 10^{-9}$ m = $2.24$ m $\approx 2.2$ m.

The dimension of a typical mammalian nucleus is approximately $10^{-6}$ m.

Thus, the approximate size of a nucleus is $10^{-6}$ m and the length of the DNA molecule is $2.2$ m.

Answer: $10^{-6}$ and 2.2

71434.text: Which one of the following conversion in glycolysis shows formation of water molecules from the substrate?
71434.sol:
In glycolysis, the conversion of 2-phosphoglycerate to phosphoenolpyruvate is catalyzed by the enzyme enolase.

This step involves the elimination of a water molecule (dehydration) from 2-phosphoglycerate to form the enol structure of phosphoenolpyruvate.

Therefore, the formation of a water molecule occurs during the conversion of 2-phosphoglycerate to phosphoenolpyruvate.

Answer: 2 Phosphoglycerate \rightarrow 2 Phosphoenolpyruvate

71756.subject: Chemistry
71756.text: Calculate the equilibrium constant at $25\ ^{}^{\circ}\text{C}$ for the cell reaction, $\text{Ni(s)} + \text{Cu}^{2+}(1\text{M}) \rightarrow \text{Ni}^{2+}(1\text{M}) + \text{Cu(s)}$ if $E^{}^{\circ}_{cell}$ is $0.592\ \text{V}$.
71756.sol:
The given cell reaction is $\text{Ni(s)} + \text{Cu}^{2+}(1\text{M}) \rightarrow \text{Ni}^{2+}(1\text{M}) + \text{Cu(s)}$.

The number of electrons transferred in the reaction is $n = 2$.

The relationship between the standard cell potential and the equilibrium constant $K_c$ at $25\ ^{}^{\circ}\text{C}$ is given by:

$E^{}^{\circ}_{cell} = \dfrac{0.0592}{n} \log K_c$

Substituting the given values:

$0.592 = \dfrac{0.0592}{2} \log K_c$

$\log K_c = \dfrac{0.592 \times 2}{0.0592}$

$\log K_c = 20$

$K_c = 10^{20} = 1.0 \times 10^{20}$

Answer: $1.0 \times 10^{20}$

71783.subject: Chemistry
71783.text: The molar conductivity of $0.8\ \text{M}\text{BaCl}_2$ solution at $25^{}^{\circ}\text{C}$ is $220\ \Omega^{-1}\text{cm}^2\text{mol}^{-1}$. Calculate its conductivity.
71783.sol:
Molar conductivity is given by the formula:

$\Lambda_m = \dfrac{\kappa \times 1000}{M}$

where $\kappa$ is the conductivity and $M$ is the molarity of the solution.

Rearranging the formula to solve for $\kappa$:

$\kappa = \dfrac{\Lambda_m \times M}{1000}$

Substituting the given values $\Lambda_m = 220\ \Omega^{-1}\text{cm}^2\text{mol}^{-1}$ and $M = 0.8\ \text{M}$:

$\kappa = \dfrac{220 \times 0.8}{1000}$

$\kappa = \dfrac{176}{1000} = 0.176\ \Omega^{-1}\text{cm}^{-1}$

Answer: $0.176\ \Omega^{-1}\text{cm}^{-1}$

72453.text: An interference is observed due to two coherent sources, A and B, separated by a distance $4\lambda$ along the Y-axis, where $\lambda$ is the wavelength of the source. A detector D is moved along the positive X-axis. The number of points on the X-axis, excluding $x = 0$ and $x \to \infty$, at which maxima will be observed, is
72453.sol:
Let source B be at $(0,0)$ and source A be at $(0, 4\lambda)$.

The path difference $\Delta p$ at a point $D(x, 0)$ on the positive X-axis is given by:

$\Delta p = AD - BD = \sqrt{x^2 + (4\lambda)^2} - x$

Let us check the boundary values of the path difference:
At $x = 0$, $\Delta p = \sqrt{0 + 16\lambda^2} - 0 = 4\lambda$.
As $x \to \infty$, $\Delta p = \lim_{x \to \infty} x\left(1 + \dfrac{16\lambda^2}{x^2}\right)^{1/2} - x = 0$.

For constructive interference (maxima), the path difference must be an integer multiple of the wavelength:

$\Delta p = n\lambda$

Since the points $x = 0$ and $x \to \infty$ are explicitly excluded, the path difference must strictly lie in the range:

$0 < \Delta p < 4\lambda$

Therefore, the possible values for $\Delta p$ are $1\lambda, 2\lambda,$ and $3\lambda$.

This corresponds to $n = 1, 2, 3$.

Thus, there are exactly $3$ points on the positive X-axis where maxima will be observed.

Answer: $3$

73791.subject: General Ability
73791.text: The position vector of a particle is given by $\vec{r} = \sqrt{3}\,t^2\hat{i} + \sqrt{2}\,t\hat{j} + \sqrt{5}\,\hat{k}$. Which one of the following statements is correct?
options: The force acting on the particle is parallel to the instantaneous momentum of the particle.
The force acting on the particle is perpendicular to the instantaneous momentum of the particle.
The force acting on the particle is not parallel to the instantaneous momentum of the particle.
73791.sol:
Given position vector $\vec{r} = \sqrt{3}t^2\hat{i} + \sqrt{2}t\hat{j} + \sqrt{5}\hat{k}$

Velocity $\vec{v} = \dfrac{d\vec{r}}{dt} = 2\sqrt{3}t\hat{i} + \sqrt{2}\hat{j}$

Instantaneous momentum $\vec{p} = m\vec{v} = m(2\sqrt{3}t\hat{i} + \sqrt{2}\hat{j})$

Acceleration $\vec{a} = \dfrac{d\vec{v}}{dt} = 2\sqrt{3}\hat{i}$

Force $\vec{F} = m\vec{a} = 2\sqrt{3}m\hat{i}$

Taking the cross product of force and momentum:

$\vec{F} \times \vec{p} = (2\sqrt{3}m\hat{i}) \times m(2\sqrt{3}t\hat{i} + \sqrt{2}\hat{j}) = 2\sqrt{6}m^2\hat{k} \neq 0$

Since the cross product is non-zero, the force is not parallel to the instantaneous momentum.

Also, $\vec{F} \cdot \vec{p} = 12m^2t \neq 0$, so they are not perpendicular either.

Answer: The force acting on the particle is not parallel to the instantaneous momentum of the particle.

75204.text:
Consider the following statements with reference to structure of the Earth's atmosphere:
1. Thickness of the troposphere is greatest at the equator
2. The air temperature of the tropopause is highest above the poles
3. The temperature in troposphere decreases at the rate of 1°F for every 165 m of height
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
75204.sol:
The thickness of the troposphere is greatest at the equator because heat is transported to great heights by strong convectional currents. Thus, statement 1 is correct.

The temperature at the tropopause over the equator is about $-80^{{}^{\circ}}\text{C}$, while over the poles it is about $-45^{{}^{\circ}}\text{C}$. Since $-45^{{}^{\circ}}\text{C}$ is greater than $-80^{{}^{\circ}}\text{C}$, the air temperature of the tropopause is highest above the poles. Thus, statement 2 is correct.

The temperature in the troposphere decreases at the rate of $1^{{}^{\circ}}\text{C}$ (not $1^{{}^{\circ}}\text{F}$) for every $165\text{ m}$ of height, which is known as the normal lapse rate. Thus, statement 3 is incorrect.

Therefore, only statements 1 and 2 are correct.

Answer: 1 and 2 only

76898.subject: Mathematics
76898.text: Let $f(x)=\begin{vmatrix} 3x^2 \text{ and } \cos x \text{ and } -\sin x \\ 6 \text{ and } -1 \text{ and } 0 \\ q \text{ and } q^2 \text{ and } q^3 \end{vmatrix}$ where $q$ is any constant, then what is $\dfrac{d^2}{dx^2}\big(f(x)\big)$ at $x=0$ equal to ?
76898.sol:
Given the function $f(x)$ as a determinant where only the first row contains the variable $x$:

$f(x)=\begin{vmatrix} 3x^2 \text{ and } \cos x \text{ and } -\sin x \\ 6 \text{ and } -1 \text{ and } 0 \\ q \text{ and } q^2 \text{ and } q^3 \end{vmatrix}$

To differentiate the determinant with respect to $x$, we differentiate the elements of the first row while keeping the other rows unchanged.

Differentiating once with respect to $x$:

$f'(x)=\begin{vmatrix} 6x \text{ and } -\sin x \text{ and } -\cos x \\ 6 \text{ and } -1 \text{ and } 0 \\ q \text{ and } q^2 \text{ and } q^3 \end{vmatrix}$

Differentiating again with respect to $x$:

$f''(x)=\begin{vmatrix} 6 \text{ and } -\cos x \text{ and } \sin x \\ 6 \text{ and } -1 \text{ and } 0 \\ q \text{ and } q^2 \text{ and } q^3 \end{vmatrix}$

Substituting $x=0$ into the second derivative:

$f''(0)=\begin{vmatrix} 6 \text{ and } -1 \text{ and } 0 \\ 6 \text{ and } -1 \text{ and } 0 \\ q \text{ and } q^2 \text{ and } q^3 \end{vmatrix}$

Since the first and second rows of the determinant are identical, the value of the determinant is zero.

$f''(0) = 0$

Answer: $0$

Given that $\int \frac{3 \cos x+4 \sin x}{2 \cos x+5 \sin x} d x=\frac{\alpha x}{29}+\frac{\beta}{29} \ln |2 \cos x+5 \sin x|+c$
What is the value of $\beta$ ?
77469.sol:
Let,
$\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{I}=\int \frac{3 \cos x+4 \sin x}{2 \cos x+5 \sin x} d x \\
& 3 \cos x+4 \sin x=\mathrm{A}(2 \cos x+5 \sin x) \\
& +\mathrm{B}\left[\frac{d}{d x}(2 \cos x+5 \sin x)\right] \\
& 3 \cos x+4 \sin x=\mathrm{A}(2 \cos x+5 \sin x) \\
& +\mathrm{B}(-2 \sin x+5 \cos x)
\end{aligned}$
Comparing co-efficient of $\sin x and \cos x\begin{aligned}
& 3=2 A+5 B \qquad ....(i)\\
& 4=5 A-2 B \qquad ....(ii)
\end{aligned}$
Solving (i) and (ii) then we get,
$\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{A}=\frac{26}{29}, \mathrm{ B}=\frac{7}{29} \\
& \mathrm{I}=\frac{\int \frac{26}{29}(2 \cos x+5 \sin x)+\frac{7}{29}(-2 \sin x+5 \cos x)}{2 \cos x+5 \sin x} d x \\
&=\int \frac{26}{29} d x+\frac{7}{29} \int \frac{(-2 \sin x+5 \cos x)}{2 \cos x+5 \sin x} d x \\
&=\frac{26}{29} x+\frac{7}{29} \text{ In }(2 \cos x+5 \sin x)+c \\
& \alpha=26, \beta=7[\text{ [on comparing] }
\end{aligned}\beta=7$

81233.text:
Which of the following does not show optical isomerism?
(en = ethylenediamine)
81233.sol:
Optical isomerism is exhibited by only those complexes in which elements of symmetry are absent. Octahedral complexes of the types $\left[\mathrm{M}(\mathrm{aa})_3\right],\left[\mathrm{M}(\mathrm{aa}) \mathrm{x}_2, \mathrm{y}_2\right]$ and $\left[\mathrm{M}(\mathrm{aa})_2 \mathrm{x}_2\right]$ have absence of elements of symmetry, thus exhibit optical isomerism. Here, $a a$ represents bidentate ligand, $x$ or $y$ represents monodentate ligand and $M$ represents central metal ion.
Hence, $\left[\mathrm{Co}\left(\mathrm{NH}_3\right)_3 \mathrm{Cl}_3\right]^0$ due to presence of symmetry elements does not exhibit optical isomerism.

84255.subject: Zoology
84255.text: Which one of the following pairs of organs includes only the endocrine glands?
84255.sol: In vertebrate body the glands may be classified on the basis of presence or absence of ducts, ie, exocrine and endocrine glands. The secretions of exocrine glands are carried by ducts to a particular organ for some metabolic activity, eg, salivary glands, liver. The endocrine glands have no ducts and their secretions get absorbed into the immediate surrounding blood circulation to reach the specific organs to initiate a particular metabolic change, eg, thyroid, parathyroid, adrenal, thymus. The glands, which have dual functions (ie, secretion of hormones and some other functions) are called heterocrine glands, $\mathrm{eg}$, pancreas, testes, ovaries.

84558.subject: Zoology
84558.text: What is true about T-lymphocytes in mammals?
options: there are three main typescytotoxic T-cells, helper T-cells and suppressor T-cells
they scavenge damaged cells and cellular debris
84558.sol:
T cells account for about \(80 \%\) of all lymphocytes. They are named T cells because they mature in the thymus, a gland found in the chest. There are three types of T cell lymphocytes:
- Cytotoxic T cell
- Suppressor T cell
- Helper T cell
Helper T cells are arguably the most important cells in adaptive immunity, as they are required for almost all adaptive immune responses. They not only help activate \(B\) cells to secrete antibodies and macrophages to destroy ingested microbes, but they also help activate cytotoxic \(T\) cells to kill infected target cells. A cytotoxic T cell is a Tlymphocyte (a type of white blood cell) that kills cancer cells, cells that are infected (particularly with viruses), or cells that are damaged in other ways. The regulatory T cells formerly known as suppressor T cells are a subpopulation of T cells that modulate the immune system, maintain tolerance to self-antigens, and prevent autoimmune disease.
So, the correct answer is 'There are three main types-cytotoxic T-cells, helper T-cells, and suppressor T-cells'.

86222.subject: Chemistry
86222.text: X, Y, and Z are three volatile liquids, which when mixed make an ideal solution. At a given temperature $T_0$, the constituents X, Y, and Z have pure vapour pressures in the ratio $3:2:1$. A mixture prepared with mole-fractions of X, Y, and Z in the ratio $1:2:3$ starts to boil at temperature $T_0$ at $1.5$ atm pressure. At temperature $T_0$, the partial vapour pressure (in atm) of Y is:
86222.sol:
Let the pure vapour pressures of X, Y, and Z be $P_X^{}^{\circ} = 3P$, $P_Y^{}^{\circ} = 2P$, and $P_Z^{}^{\circ} = P$.

The mole fractions of X, Y, and Z in the mixture are:
$x_X = \dfrac{1}{1+2+3} = \dfrac{1}{6}$
$x_Y = \dfrac{2}{6} = \dfrac{1}{3}$
$x_Z = \dfrac{3}{6} = \dfrac{1}{2}$

According to Raoult's law, the total vapour pressure of the ideal solution is:
$P_{total} = x_X P_X^{}^{\circ} + x_Y P_Y^{}^{\circ} + x_Z P_Z^{}^{\circ}$

Substituting the values:
$P_{total} = \left(\dfrac{1}{6}\right)(3P) + \left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)(2P) + \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)(P)$
$P_{total} = \dfrac{P}{2} + \dfrac{2P}{3} + \dfrac{P}{2} = \dfrac{5P}{3}$

Since the mixture boils at $T_0$ at $1.5$ atm pressure, the total vapour pressure is $1.5$ atm.
$\dfrac{5P}{3} = 1.5 = \dfrac{3}{2}$
$P = \dfrac{9}{10}$ atm

The partial vapour pressure of Y is:
$P_Y = x_Y P_Y^{}^{\circ} = \dfrac{2P}{3}$

Substituting the value of $P$:
$P_Y = \dfrac{2}{3} \times \dfrac{9}{10} = \dfrac{3}{5}$ atm

Answer: $\dfrac{3}{5}$

86907.subject: Physics
86907.text: One mole of a monatomic ideal gas undergoes a transformation from an initial state with temperature $290$ K and volume $30$ litres to a final state with temperature $310$ K and volume $16$ litres. On the pressure–volume (P - V$) diagram, this process is represented by a straight line path. The magnitude of the work done (in joules) during this process is close to$
86907.sol:
For a straight line path on the $P-V$ diagram, the work done is given by the area of the trapezium under the curve:

$W = \dfrac{1}{2}(P_1 + P_2)(V_2 - V_1)$

The magnitude of the work done is:

$|W| = \dfrac{1}{2}(P_1 + P_2)|V_2 - V_1|$

Using the ideal gas equation $P = \dfrac{nRT}{V}$ for $n = 1$ mole:

$P_1 = \dfrac{RT_1}{V_1} = \dfrac{8.314 \times 290}{30 \times 10^{-3}} = 80.368 \times 10^3 \text{ Pa}$

$P_2 = \dfrac{RT_2}{V_2} = \dfrac{8.314 \times 310}{16 \times 10^{-3}} = 161.083 \times 10^3 \text{ Pa}$

The change in volume is:

$|V_2 - V_1| = |16 - 30| \times 10^{-3} = 14 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m}^3$

Substituting these values into the work done formula:

$|W| = \dfrac{1}{2} (80.368 \times 10^3 + 161.083 \times 10^3) \times 14 \times 10^{-3}$

$|W| = \dfrac{1}{2} (241.451 \times 10^3) \times 14 \times 10^{-3}$

$|W| = 241.451 \times 7 \approx 1690 \text{ J}$

Answer: $1690$

$⇒ 4a + 2b + c = 0$
Also, $a, b, c$ are in A.P.

$2b = a + c$
$⇒ 4a + a + c + c = 0$
$⇒ 5a = - 2c$
$⇒ \dfrac{c}{a} = - \dfrac{5}{2} = 2 \times \alpha$
$⇒ \alpha = - \dfrac{5}{4}.$

100679.subject: Physics
100679.text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): A block takes twice the time to slide down a rough $45^{\circ}$ inclined plane as compared to a perfectly smooth $45^{\circ}$ inclined plane of the same length. The coefficient of kinetic friction for the rough plane is $0.75$.

Reason (R): The coefficient of kinetic friction between two given surfaces is independent of the macroscopic area of contact.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false but Reason (R) is true.
100679.sol:
Assertion (A) is true: Let the length of the incline be $L$. The acceleration on the smooth incline is $a_S = g \sin 45^{\circ}$. The acceleration on the rough incline is $a_R = g(\sin 45^{\circ} - \mu_k \cos 45^{\circ})$.

Using $L = \dfrac{1}{2} a t^2$, we get $t = \sqrt{\dfrac{2L}{a}}$.

Given $t_R = 2 t_S$, we have:
$\sqrt{\dfrac{2L}{a_R}} = 2 \sqrt{\dfrac{2L}{a_S}}$
$\Rightarrow a_S = 4 a_R$

Substituting the accelerations:
$g \sin 45^{\circ} = 4 g(\sin 45^{\circ} - \mu_k \cos 45^{\circ})$

Since $\sin 45^{\circ} = \cos 45^{\circ}$, this simplifies to:
$1 = 4(1 - \mu_k)$
$\Rightarrow 1 = 4 - 4\mu_k \Rightarrow 4\mu_k = 3 \Rightarrow \mu_k = 0.75$.

Reason (R) is true: The laws of friction state that the coefficient of kinetic friction is independent of the apparent macroscopic area of contact between the surfaces.

However, Reason (R) does not explain Assertion (A), as the calculation of $\mu_k$ depends on the kinematic relationship between time and acceleration ($t \propto \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{a}}$), not on the area of contact.

Answer: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).

101014.subject: Physics
101014.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
101014.text: A moving object of mass $3\text{ kg}$ and velocity $(4\hat{i} + 4\hat{j})\text{ m/s}$ breaks into two pieces of masses $1\text{ kg}$ and $2\text{ kg}$. If the $1\text{ kg}$ piece moves with a velocity of $(4\hat{i} - 2\hat{j})\text{ m/s}$ immediately after the explosion, the kinetic energy released during the explosion is
101014.sol:
By the principle of conservation of linear momentum:
$\vec{P}_{initial} = \vec{P}_{final}$
$M\vec{v} = m_1\vec{v}_1 + m_2\vec{v}_2$

Substituting the given values:
$3(4\hat{i} + 4\hat{j}) = 1(4\hat{i} - 2\hat{j}) + 2\vec{v}_2$
$12\hat{i} + 12\hat{j} = 4\hat{i} - 2\hat{j} + 2\vec{v}_2$
$2\vec{v}_2 = (12 - 4)\hat{i} + (12 + 2)\hat{j}$
$2\vec{v}_2 = 8\hat{i} + 14\hat{j}$
$\vec{v}_2 = 4\hat{i} + 7\hat{j}\text{ m/s}$

Now, calculate the initial kinetic energy ($K_i$):
$K_i = \dfrac{1}{2} M |\vec{v}|^2 = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 3 \times (4^2 + 4^2) = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 3 \times 32 = 48\text{ J}$

Calculate the final kinetic energy ($K_f$):
$K_f = \dfrac{1}{2} m_1 |\vec{v}_1|^2 + \dfrac{1}{2} m_2 |\vec{v}_2|^2$
$K_f = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 1 \times (4^2 + (-2)^2) + \dfrac{1}{2} \times 2 \times (4^2 + 7^2)$
$K_f = \dfrac{1}{2}(16 + 4) + 1(16 + 49)$
$K_f = 10 + 65 = 75\text{ J}$

The kinetic energy released in the explosion is the increase in kinetic energy:
$\Delta K = K_f - K_i = 75\text{ J} - 48\text{ J} = 27\text{ J}$.

Answer: $27\text{ J}$

102802.subject: Physics
102802.text: Six point charges, each of the same magnitude $q$, are arranged in different manners as shown in Column-II. In each case, a point $M$ and a line $P Q$ passing through $M$ are shown. Let $E$ be the electric field and $V$ be the electric potential at $M$ (potential at infinity is zero) due to the given charge distribution when it is at rest. Now, the whole system is set into rotation with a constant angular velocity about the line $P Q$. Let $B$ the magnetic field at $M$ and $\mu$ be the magnetic moment of the system in this condition. Assume each rotating charge to be equivalent to a steady current.
102802.sol:
Concise justification (one line per match):
- A: \(E=0  → p, r, s\).
Each of these arrangements is point-symmetric about \(M\) so the vector sum of electric fields cancels at \(M\) : (p) alternating charges on a regular hexagon, (r) concentric rings with symmetric charge placement, (s) symmetrical rectangle with charges at corners/midpoints.
- B: \(V  ≠ 0 $\rightarrow \mathrm{r}$\), s.
Potential is a scalar sum and need not cancel even if fields cancel; in (\(r\)) and (\(s\)) the positive and negative charges sit at different radii/positions so the net scalar potential at \(M\) is nonzero.
- C: \(B=0 $\rightarrow \mathrm{p}, \mathrm{q}, \mathrm{t}$\).
When the whole system rotates about the shown axis the circulating currents from oppositely-signed charges cancel pairwise in these configurations, giving zero magnetic field at \(M\).
- \($\mathrm{D}$: \mu $\neq \mathrm{0} \rightarrow \mathrm{r}, \mathrm{s}$\).
In (r) and (s) the rotating charges produce unequal effective current loops (different radii or an unbalanced loop geometry), so a net magnetic moment remains.
Hence choice (3).

102916.subject: Physics
102916.text: Sixty-four identical spherical liquid drops, each carrying the same charge, coalesce to form a single large drop. What is the ratio of the total initial electrostatic energy of all the small drops to the final electrostatic energy of the large drop?
102916.sol:
Let the charge on each small drop be $q$ and its radius be $r$. The electrostatic energy of one small drop is $U_{\text{small}} = \dfrac{kq^2}{2r}$.

For $N = 64$ such drops, the total initial energy is:
$U_i = N \times U_{\text{small}} = 64 \times \dfrac{kq^2}{2r}$

When they coalesce, the total charge of the large drop is $Q = Nq = 64q$.
By conservation of volume, the radius $R$ of the large drop is:
$\dfrac{4}{3}\pi R^3 = 64 \times \dfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3 \Rightarrow R = 64^{1/3}r = 4r$

The final electrostatic energy of the large drop is:
$U_f = \dfrac{kQ^2}{2R} = \dfrac{k(64q)^2}{2(4r)} = \dfrac{4096}{4} \times \dfrac{kq^2}{2r} = 1024 \times \dfrac{kq^2}{2r}$

The ratio of total initial energy to final energy is:
$\dfrac{U_i}{U_f} = \dfrac{64}{1024} = \dfrac{1}{16}$

Thus, the required ratio is $1:16$.

Answer: $1:16$

103183.subject: Physics
103183.text: A capacitor having capacitance $1 \mu \mathrm{F}$ with air, is filled with two dielectrics as shown. How many times capacitance will increase?
103183.sol: Key Idea : After filling with dielectrics the two capacitors will be in parallel order. As shown, the two capacitors are connected in parallel. Initially the capacitance of capacitor $C=\frac{\varepsilon_0 A}{d}$ where $A$ is area of each plate and $d$ is the separation between the plates. After filling with dielectrics, we have two capacitors of capacitance. $C_1=\frac{K_1 \varepsilon_0(A / 2)}{d}=\frac{8}{2} \frac{\varepsilon_0 A}{d}=\frac{4 \varepsilon_0 A}{d}=4 C and C_2=\frac{K_2 \varepsilon_0(A / 2)}{d}=\frac{4}{2} \frac{\varepsilon_0 A}{d}=\frac{2 \varepsilon_0 A}{d}=2 C$ Hence, their equivalent capacitance $\begin{aligned} C_{\mathrm{eq}} & =C_1+C_2 \\ & =4 C+2 C=6 C\end{aligned}$ ie, new capacitance will be six times of the original.

103313.subject: Physics
103313.text:
Four different Wheatstone bridge configurations, labelled I, II, III, and IV, are initially in a balanced state. The resistance values of the four arms $P$, $Q$, $R$, and $S$ for each configuration are given in the table below.

Bridge$P$ ($\Omega$)$Q$ ($\Omega$)$R$ ($\Omega$)$S$ ($\Omega$)
I$10$$10$$10$$10$
II$1000$$1000$$1000$$1000$
III$100$$1$$100$$1$
IV$1$$100$$1$$100$


If the resistance $S$ is increased by exactly $0.1\text{ }\Omega$ in all four setups, which bridge will show the maximum deflection in the galvanometer? (Assume the same battery and galvanometer are used in all cases).
103313.sol:
The sensitivity of a Wheatstone bridge is defined by the deflection in the galvanometer for a small fractional change in resistance.

A bridge is most sensitive when the resistances of all four arms are of the same order of magnitude (i.e., $P \approx Q \approx R \approx S$). This eliminates Bridges III and IV, which have highly unequal ratio arms.

Furthermore, for a given small unbalance, a bridge with smaller absolute resistance values draws more current from the battery, leading to a larger Thevenin equivalent voltage and current across the galvanometer. Therefore, Bridge I ($10\text{ }\Omega$ in all arms) will be more sensitive than Bridge II ($1000\text{ }\Omega$ in all arms) and will show the maximum deflection.

Answer: Bridge I

103696.subject: Physics
103696.text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): For a uniform circular loop carrying a steady current that enters at point P and leaves at point Q, the net magnetic field at the center is always zero for any position of P and Q.
Reason (R): The current divides into the two segments of the loop in direct proportion to their lengths.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both Assertion and Reason are true and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Assertion is false but Reason is true.
103696.sol:
Let the total current entering the uniform circular loop be $I$. The loop is divided into two segments of lengths $L_1$ and $L_2$, subtending angles $\theta_1$ and $\theta_2$ at the center, respectively.

Since the loop is uniform, the resistance of each segment is proportional to its length (and thus its subtended angle). Therefore, $R_1 \propto \theta_1$ and $R_2 \propto \theta_2$.

In a parallel combination, the current divides in the inverse ratio of the resistances. Thus, the currents in the two segments are $I_1 = I \dfrac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2} = I \dfrac{\theta_2}{2\pi}$ and $I_2 = I \dfrac{R_1}{R_1 + R_2} = I \dfrac{\theta_1}{2\pi}$.

This shows that the current divides in the inverse proportion to their lengths, making the Reason (R) false.

The magnetic field at the center due to the first segment is $B_1 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I_1}{4\pi r} \theta_1 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi r} \dfrac{\theta_1 \theta_2}{2\pi}$.

The magnetic field at the center due to the second segment is $B_2 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I_2}{4\pi r} \theta_2 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi r} \dfrac{\theta_1 \theta_2}{2\pi}$.

Since the currents flow in opposite angular directions, their magnetic fields at the center are in opposite directions. The net magnetic field is $B_{net} = B_1 - B_2 = 0$.

This holds true regardless of the positions of the entry and exit points P and Q. Thus, the Assertion (A) is true.

Therefore, Assertion is true but Reason is false.

Answer: Assertion is true but Reason is false.

104107.subject: Physics
104107.text: An ideal inductor of inductance $L$ is connected across an alternating voltage source. If the instantaneous voltage is given by $V = V_0 \sin(\omega t)$, what is the expression for the instantaneous current $I$ flowing through the circuit?
104107.sol:
In a purely inductive circuit, the current lags behind the voltage by a phase angle of $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

Given the voltage $V = V_0 \sin(\omega t)$, the phase of the current can be written as:
$I = I_0 \sin\left(\omega t - \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$

The peak current $I_0$ is related to the peak voltage $V_0$ by the inductive reactance $X_L = \omega L$:
$I_0 = \dfrac{V_0}{X_L} = \dfrac{V_0}{\omega L}$

Substituting $I_0$ into the current expression:
$I = \dfrac{V_0}{\omega L} \sin\left(\omega t - \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$

Using the trigonometric identity $\sin(\theta - \dfrac{\pi}{2}) = -\cos(\theta)$, we get:
$I = -\dfrac{V_0}{\omega L} \cos(\omega t)$

Answer: $-\dfrac{V_0}{\omega L} \cos(\omega t)$

104131.subject: Physics
104131.text: A series LCR circuit is connected to an AC source of rms voltage $130\ \text{V}$. The circuit components have a resistance of $12\ \Omega$, an inductive reactance of $14\ \Omega$, and a capacitive reactance of $9\ \Omega$. What will be the reading of an ideal AC voltmeter connected strictly across the series combination of the inductor and the capacitor?
104131.sol:
First, calculate the net impedance $Z$ of the series LCR circuit:

$Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}$

Substitute the given values ($R = 12\ \Omega$, $X_L = 14\ \Omega$, $X_C = 9\ \Omega$):

$Z = \sqrt{12^2 + (14 - 9)^2}$
$Z = \sqrt{144 + 5^2}$
$Z = \sqrt{144 + 25} = \sqrt{169} = 13\ \Omega$

Next, find the rms current $I_{\text{rms}}$ flowing through the circuit using Ohm's law for AC circuits:

$I_{\text{rms}} = \dfrac{V_{\text{rms}}}{Z} = \dfrac{130\ \text{V}}{13\ \Omega} = 10\ \text{A}$

An ideal AC voltmeter connected across the inductor and capacitor combination will measure the net rms voltage across them. The net reactance of the LC combination is:

$X_{\text{LC}} = |X_L - X_C| = |14 - 9| = 5\ \Omega$

The voltage reading $V_{\text{LC}}$ across this combination is:

$V_{\text{LC}} = I_{\text{rms}} \times X_{\text{LC}} = 10\ \text{A} \times 5\ \Omega = 50\ \text{V}$

Answer: $50\ \text{V}$

104693.subject: Physics
104693.text:
Match List-I with List-II regarding the interference pattern produced by two coherent sources:

List-I (Path/Phase difference)List-II (Fringe type)
(A) $\Delta x = 0$(I) First minimum
(B) $\Delta x = \dfrac{\lambda}{2}$(II) Central maximum
(C) $\Delta \phi = 2\pi$(III) Third minimum
(D) $\Delta \phi = 5\pi$(IV) First maximum

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
104693.sol:
The phase difference $\Delta \phi$ and path difference $\Delta x$ are related by $\Delta \phi = \dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda} \Delta x$.

For (A): $\Delta x = 0$ corresponds to a phase difference of zero, which is the condition for the central maximum. Hence, (A) matches with (II).

For (B): $\Delta x = \dfrac{\lambda}{2}$ corresponds to $\Delta \phi = \pi$. This satisfies the condition for the first minimum, $\Delta \phi = (2n-1)\pi$ with $n=1$. Hence, (B) matches with (I).

For (C): $\Delta \phi = 2\pi$ satisfies the condition for constructive interference $\Delta \phi = 2n\pi$ with $n=1$, which is the first maximum. Hence, (C) matches with (IV).

For (D): $\Delta \phi = 5\pi$ satisfies the condition for destructive interference $\Delta \phi = (2n-1)\pi$ with $n=3$, which is the third minimum. Hence, (D) matches with (III).

The correct matching is (A)-(II), (B)-(I), (C)-(IV), (D)-(III).

Answer: (A)-(II), (B)-(I), (C)-(IV), (D)-(III)

$\left(R=1.09 \times 10^7 \mathrm{~m}^{-1}\right)$

112647.text: Chlorination of benzene in the presence of anhydrous $\text{AlCl}_3$ yields a mixture of disubstituted isomers X and Y. Isomer Y has a significantly higher melting point than X and is easily separated by crystallization. Identify isomer Y and the primary reason for its higher melting point.
options: $p$-Dichlorobenzene; symmetry leading to better crystal lattice packing
$o$-Dichlorobenzene; higher dipole moment leading to stronger dipole-dipole interactions
$p$-Dichlorobenzene; presence of strong intermolecular hydrogen bonding
$m$-Dichlorobenzene; lower steric hindrance between the chlorine atoms
112647.sol:
Chlorination of benzene in the presence of a Lewis acid yields a mixture of $o$-dichlorobenzene and $p$-dichlorobenzene as the major disubstituted products.

The para-isomer ($p$-dichlorobenzene) has a significantly higher melting point than the ortho-isomer. This is because the $p$-isomer is highly symmetrical, which allows its molecules to pack more closely and efficiently in the crystal lattice.

As a result of this close packing, stronger intermolecular forces exist in the crystal lattice of the para-isomer, requiring more energy to melt it. Chlorine atoms attached to a benzene ring do not form hydrogen bonds.

Answer: $p$-Dichlorobenzene; symmetry leading to better crystal lattice packing

114918.subject: Chemistry
114918.text:
For a certain chemical reaction, the plot of $\ln k$ versus $\dfrac{1}{T}$ is a straight line with a slope of $-1.0 \times 10^4 \text{ K}$. What is the activation energy of the reaction?
(Given $R = 8.314 \text{ J K}^{-1} \text{ mol}^{-1}$)
114918.sol:
According to the Arrhenius equation:
$k = A e^{-E_a / RT}$

Taking the natural logarithm on both sides yields:
$\ln k = \ln A - \dfrac{E_a}{RT}$

This represents the equation of a straight line ($y = mx + c$), where $y = \ln k$ and $x = \dfrac{1}{T}$.
The slope ($m$) of this line is $-\dfrac{E_a}{R}$.

Equating the given slope to the theoretical expression:
$-\dfrac{E_a}{R} = -1.0 \times 10^4 \text{ K}$
$E_a = 1.0 \times 10^4 \times 8.314 \text{ J mol}^{-1}$
$E_a = 83140 \text{ J mol}^{-1} = 83.14 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$

Using the factor $2.303$ is a common mistake that occurs when confusing the $\ln k$ plot with a $\log k$ plot.

Answer: $83.14 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$

Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Reduction of methyl 4-oxopentanoate with $\text{NaBH}_4$ yields methyl 4-hydroxypentanoate.
Reason (R): $\text{NaBH}_4$ is a strong reducing agent that readily reduces ester groups to primary alcohols.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A)
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A)
Assertion (A) is true but Reason (R) is false
Assertion (A) is false but Reason (R) is true
119295.sol:
Assertion (A) is true because $\text{NaBH}_4$ is a chemoselective reducing agent that reduces ketones to secondary alcohols while leaving ester groups intact. Thus, the ketone group at C-4 in methyl 4-oxopentanoate is reduced to a secondary alcohol, forming methyl 4-hydroxypentanoate.

Reason (R) is false because $\text{NaBH}_4$ is a mild reducing agent and does not reduce esters, carboxylic acids, or amides. Stronger reducing agents like $\text{LiAlH}_4$ are required to reduce esters to primary alcohols.

Answer: Assertion (A) is true but Reason (R) is false

123227.subject: Botany
123227.text: What is the outermost layer of a typical young dicotyledonous stem?
123227.sol: The transverse section of a typical young dicotyledonous stem shows that the epidermis is the outermost protective layer of the stem Covered with a thin layer of cuticle, it may bear trichomes and a few stomata. The cells arranged in multiple layers between epidermis and pericycle constitute the cortex. It consists of three sub-zones. The outer hypodermis, consists of a few layers of collenchymatous cells just below the epidermis, which provide mechanical strength to the young stem. Cortical layers below hypodermis consist of rounded thin walle parenchymatous cells with conspicuous intercellular spaces. The innermost layer of the cortex is called the endodermis. The cells of the endodermis are rich in starch grains and the layer is also referred to as the starch sheath. Pericycle is present on the inner side of the endodermis and above the phloem in the form of semi-lunar patches of sclerenchyma. In between the vascular bundles there are a few layers of radially placed parenchymatous cells, which constitute medullary rays. A large number of vascular bundles are arranged in a ring ; the ‘ring’ arrangement of vascular bundles is a characteristic of dicot stem. Each vascular bundle is conjoint, open, and with endarch protoxylem. A large number of rounded, parenchymatous cells with large intercellularspaces which occupy the central portion of the stem constitute the pith.

124271.subject: Botany
124271.text:
Read the following features of a specific cellular structure:
Membrane 'M' is a component of a double-membrane bound organelle and is relatively less permeable. The compartment 'Y' enclosed by membrane 'M' contains enzymes required for the synthesis of carbohydrates and proteins, along with 70S ribosomes.

Identify membrane 'M' and compartment 'Y'.
options: M = Inner mitochondrial membrane, Y = Matrix
M = Inner chloroplast membrane, Y = Stroma
M = Outer chloroplast membrane, Y = Stroma
M = Inner chloroplast membrane, Y = Grana
124271.sol:
According to NCERT, chloroplasts are double-membrane bound organelles. Of the two membranes, the inner chloroplast membrane is relatively less permeable. The space limited by the inner membrane of the chloroplast is called the stroma. The stroma contains enzymes required for the synthesis of carbohydrates and proteins, as well as 70S ribosomes and circular DNA.

The inner mitochondrial membrane encloses the matrix, but the matrix does not primarily synthesize carbohydrates. The outer chloroplast membrane is more permeable than the inner one. The grana are membranous structures located within the stroma, not the compartment enclosing the enzymes.

Answer: M = Inner chloroplast membrane, Y = Stroma

125344.subject: Botany
125344.text: Which pigment can appear yellow to yellow-orange in the chromatogram?
125344.sol: Looking at plants have you ever wondered why and how there are so many shades of green in their leaves – even in the same plant?
